title: Denarius of Tiberius (the 'tribute penny')
summary: A silver coin about 19 mm across and 1.5 mm thick, weighing roughly 3.8–3.9 g. Obverse: laureate head of Tiberius with TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS; reverse: a seated female figure (Livia as Pax) with PONTIF MAXIM. The relief here is schematic — the proportions are what the model is for; see the photograph on the Insights card for the real portrait.

sources.title: RIC I² Tiberius 26/30; British Museum R.6195 (BMC 49)
sources.note: the Portable Antiquities Scheme photo of BMC 49 shows the type; diameters of recorded specimens cluster at 18–19 mm

sources.title: The Metallurgy of Roman Silver Coinage
sources.author: K. Butcher & M. Ponting
sources.note: weight standard 1/84 lb (≈3.9 g) under Augustus and Tiberius

title: Alabastron — the perfume flask
summary: A calcite flask of the classic shape: rounded base (it was stood in a ring or held), narrow neck, and a flat disc lip for wiping the last drop across the skin. Mark says the woman 'broke' it — snapping the sealed neck. The height modelled here (18 cm) is a typical size; the Gospels give no dimensions, and a Roman pound of nard (John 12:3) would need a flask towards the larger end of the range.

media.caption: Calcite alabastron, Egypt, Ptolemaic period (305–31 BC), LACMA M.73.5.353

sources.title: Alabastra in the LACMA, British Museum and Israel Museum collections, Hellenistic–early Roman

title: Tyrian shekel (tetradrachm) — the temple's silver
summary: The coin the temple tax had to be paid in: about 26 mm across, 3 mm thick, 14 g of high-grade silver — four times a denarius. Obverse: head of the god Melqart-Heracles; reverse: an eagle with the legend ΤΥΡΟΥ ΙΕΡΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΑΣΥΛΟΥ, 'of Tyre, holy and inviolable'. The stater in the fish's mouth (Matthew 17:27) was one of these; Judas's thirty pieces may have been.

sources.title: Tyrian shekels, 126/5 BC – AD 65/6
sources.note: Y. Meshorer, A Treasury of Jewish Coins (2001), ch. on Tyrian coinage; the Isfiya hoard (1960) of c. 4,500 shekels and half-shekels

title: Ark of the covenant — built as the text describes it
summary: Read or play Exodus 25:10–22 (the instructions) or 37:1–9 (Bezalel making it) and the ark builds up verse by verse: the acacia chest, its gold overlay and molding, the rings, the poles, the Testimony, the mercy seat, and the cherubim with their wings. Elsewhere it is shown whole. The text gives only the chest (2½ × 1½ × 1½ cubits) and the cover (2½ × 1½); the metric size assumes a common cubit of ≈44.5 cm. Everything else, from the cover's thickness to the look of the cherubim, is reconstructed, and each such step says what it rests on.

steps.basis: the text says a molding goes 'around it' but not where; it is placed at the top edge, where it would frame the cover
'its four feet' (BSB) puts the rings low; the Hebrew pa'am can also mean 'corner', so some reconstructions set them higher. Ring size is not given
pole length and thickness are not given; modelled at ≈4½ cubits so they stand out at both ends
the Testimony is the two stone tablets (Exod 31:18); their size is not given, so they are sized to lie inside
length and width are in the text; the thickness of one handbreadth (⅙ cubit) is the Talmud's inference, b. Sukkah 5a
the text gives no form, height or posture for the cherubim; these are schematic figures, leaning in to face each other (v. 20)
the wings 'spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat'; their size and shape are not given, so the tips are drawn nearly meeting over the centre
molding placed at the top edge; the text does not say where it runs
rings set low, at the 'feet'; the Hebrew pa'am can also mean 'corner'
thickness of one handbreadth from b. Sukkah 5a
form of the cherubim not given; schematic
wing size and shape not given

sources.note: the instructions: chest and cover dimensions, overlay, molding, rings, poles, Testimony, cherubim
the same ark made by Bezalel; the Testimony is put in only at Exod 40:20

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 5a
sources.note: infers the cover was one handbreadth thick, noting that 'the Torah never states its dimensions explicitly'

sources.title: Weights and Measures of the Bible
sources.author: R. B. Y. Scott
sources.note: The Biblical Archaeologist 22, 22–40; the common cubit of ≈17.5 in (≈44.5 cm) used for the metric conversion
